title: Problem-Solving Strategies
lead: Every problem about forces is worked in the same way, and this section sets out the four steps: sketch the situation and draw each force as an arrow, list what is known and what has to be found and carefully determine the system of interest, apply Newton’s second law to the free-body diagram, and check that the answer and its units are reasonable. It also settles what has to be decided before any equation is written, which is the direction in which the system accelerates, since where the acceleration is zero along an axis the net force along that axis is zero as well.
objectives: Understand and apply a problem-solving procedure to solve problems using Newton’s laws of motion.
summary_html:
• To solve problems involving Newton’s laws of motion, follow the procedure described:
    1. Draw a sketch of the problem.
    2. Identify known and unknown quantities, and identify the system of interest. Draw a free-body diagram, which is a sketch showing all of the forces acting on an object. The object is represented by a dot, and the forces are represented by vectors extending in different directions from the dot. If vectors act in directions that are not horizontal or vertical, resolve the vectors into horizontal and vertical components and draw them on the free-body diagram.
    3. Write Newton’s second law in the horizontal and vertical directions and add the forces acting on the object. If the object does not accelerate in a particular direction (for example, the $x$-direction) then $\kFnetx = 0$. If the object does accelerate in that direction, $\kFnetx = m\ka$.
    4. Check your answer. Is the answer reasonable? Are the units correct?
notes: Problems 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12 to 17, among them the two Construct Your Own Problem items and the two Unreasonable Results items, have no answer in the book’s key and are left out, and the free-body diagrams the book draws inside the solutions of problems 1, 3 and 11 are left out with them, since a card carries the figure its problem refers to and those solutions state the same equations in words.
exercise_notes: Bloom levels, concept tags, weights and hints are AI-generated. Answers come from the book’s answer key, which covers the odd-numbered problems of the section; problems 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12 to 17 have no keyed answer and are left out, and the two Construct Your Own Problem items and the two Unreasonable Results items are among them. Of the three AP test prep items the book keys the toboggan and the free-body diagram items, and it leaves the mass hanging in the elevator unkeyed, so that one is kept as an open item with its four options as the book prints them and an AI-written suggested approach, marked as such. The book draws five figures inside the problems of this section and none of them carries a number; the two that belong to keyed problems, the snow saucer sled and the braces on a tooth, ride on their cards, and the other three belong to problems that are left out. Nothing is held for a later section and nothing is taken from another one: every item here is answered with Newton’s second law and the forces the chapter has already named. Numeric answers accept 2% tolerance.

figures.original_caption: (a) A sketch of Tarzan hanging from a vine. (b) Arrows are used to represent all forces. T is the tension in the vine above Tarzan, F_T is the force he exerts on the vine, and w is his weight. All other forces, such as the nudge of a breeze, are assumed negligible. (c) Suppose we are given the ape man’s mass and asked to find the tension in the vine. We then define the system of interest as shown and draw a free-body diagram. F_T is no longer shown, because it is not a force acting on the system of interest; rather, F_T acts on the outside world. (d) Showing only the arrows, the head-to-tail method of addition is used. It is apparent that T = −w, if Tarzan is stationary.

exercises.prompt: A toboggan with two riders has a total mass of 85.0 kg. A third person is pushing with a force of 42.5 N in the direction of motion on a toboggan moving on a sloped surface at the top of a hill that has a downward angle of 15°. The force of friction on the toboggan is 31.0 N. Which statement describes an accurate free-body diagram to represent the situation?

options: An arrow of magnitude 10.5 N points down the slope of the hill.
An arrow of magnitude 833 N points straight down.
An arrow of magnitude 833 N points perpendicular to the slope of the hill.
An arrow of magnitude 73.5 N points down the slope of the hill.
answer.hint: Each arrow of a free-body diagram is one external force, not a sum of several. One of the four numbers is the weight of the toboggan and its riders, and a weight always points straight down.

exercises.prompt:
A mass of 2.0 kg is suspended from the ceiling of an elevator by a rope. What is the tension in the rope when the elevator (i) accelerates upward at $1.5\ \text{m/s}^2$? (ii) accelerates downward at $1.5\ \text{m/s}^2$?
  1. (i) 22.6 N; (ii) 16.6 N
  2. Because the mass is hanging from the elevator itself, the tension in the rope will not change in either case.
  3. (i) 22.6 N; (ii) 19.6 N
  4. (i) 16.6 N; (ii) 19.6 N

answer.solution: Take the hanging mass alone as the system of interest and draw its free-body diagram: the tension pulls up along the rope and the weight pulls down, and there is nothing else. The mass is carried by the elevator, so it has the elevator’s acceleration, and along the vertical axis the acceleration is not zero. Newton’s second law along that axis therefore reads $F_{\text{net}\,y} = T - w = ma$, so the tension is the weight plus $ma$ when the acceleration is upward and the weight minus $ma$ when it is downward. Work out the weight of the 2.0 kg mass and the product of its mass and 1.5 m/s², and look for the option whose two readings sit the same distance above and below the weight. Checking the answer, an option in which the tension does not change at all cannot be right, since a changed acceleration needs a changed net force.

exercises.prompt: Which statement is true about drawing free-body diagrams?

options: Drawing a free-body diagram should be the last step in solving a problem about forces.
Drawing a free-body diagram helps you compare forces quantitatively.
The forces in a free-body diagram should always balance.
Drawing a free-body diagram can help you determine the net force.
answer.hint: Ask what the diagram is for. It gathers every external force on the system in one drawing, before any equation is written, and the forces on it balance only when the system is not accelerating.

exercises.prompt: A $5.00\times 10^{5}\text{-kg}$ rocket is accelerating straight up. Its engines produce $1.250\times 10^{7}\ \text{N}$ of thrust, and air resistance is $4.50\times 10^{6}\ \text{N}$. What is the rocket’s acceleration? Explicitly show how you follow the steps in the Problem-Solving Strategy for Newton’s laws of motion.

answer.hint: Take the rocket as the system of interest. Three external forces act along the vertical axis: the thrust up, the air resistance down and the weight down.
answer.solution: Using the free-body diagram: $F_{\text{net}} = T - f - mg = ma$, so that $a = \dfrac{T - f - mg}{m} = \dfrac{1.250\times 10^{7}\ \text{N} - 4.50\times 10^{6}\ \text{N} - (5.00\times 10^{5}\ \text{kg})(9.80\ \text{m/s}^2)}{5.00\times 10^{5}\ \text{kg}} = 6.20\ \text{m/s}^2$.

exercises.prompt: Calculate the force a 70.0-kg high jumper must exert on the ground to produce an upward acceleration 4.00 times the acceleration due to gravity. Explicitly show how you follow the steps in the Problem-Solving Strategy for Newton’s laws of motion.

answer.hint: The jumper accelerates upward, so the net force along the vertical axis is $ma$ and is the upward force from the ground less his weight.
answer.solution: 1. Use Newton’s laws of motion. 2. Given: $a = 4.00g = (4.00)(9.80\ \text{m/s}^2) = 39.2\ \text{m/s}^2$; $m = 70.0\ \text{kg}$. Find: $F$. 3. $\sum F = +F - w = ma$, so that $F = ma + w = ma + mg = m(a + g)$. $F = (70.0\ \text{kg})[(39.2\ \text{m/s}^2) + (9.80\ \text{m/s}^2)] = 3.43\times 10^{3}\ \text{N}$. The force exerted by the high-jumper is actually down on the ground, but $F$ is up from the ground and makes him jump. 4. This result is reasonable, since it is quite possible for a person to exert a force of the magnitude of $10^{3}\ \text{N}$.

exercises.prompt: A freight train consists of two $8.00\times 10^{4}\text{-kg}$ engines and 45 cars with average masses of $5.50\times 10^{4}\ \text{kg}$. (a) What force must each engine exert backward on the track to accelerate the train at a rate of $5.00\times 10^{-2}\ \text{m/s}^2$ if the force of friction is $7.50\times 10^{5}\ \text{N}$, assuming the engines exert identical forces? This is not a large frictional force for such a massive system. Rolling friction for trains is small, and consequently trains are very energy-efficient transportation systems. (b) What is the force in the coupling between the 37th and 38th cars (this is the force each exerts on the other), assuming all cars have the same mass and that friction is evenly distributed among all of the cars and engines?

parts.hint: Take the whole train as the system of interest, add the masses of the two engines and the 45 cars, and remember that the two engines share the forward force equally.
Now take the part of the train behind the coupling as the system of interest: the coupling force and that part’s share of the friction are the only external forces along the track.

exercises.prompt: A 1100-kg car pulls a boat on a trailer. (a) What total force resists the motion of the car, boat, and trailer, if the car exerts a 1900-N force on the road and produces an acceleration of $0.550\ \text{m/s}^2$? The mass of the boat plus trailer is 700 kg. (b) What is the force in the hitch between the car and the trailer if 80% of the resisting forces are experienced by the boat and trailer?

parts.hint: Take the car, the boat and the trailer together as the system of interest, so that the hitch force is internal and drops out.
Change the system of interest to the boat and trailer alone; the hitch force and their share of the resisting force are then the external forces along the road.

figure.alt: An overhead view of a child sitting on a snow saucer sled. Two forces, F sub one equal to ten newtons and F sub two equal to eight newtons, are acting toward the right. F sub one makes an angle of forty-five degrees from the x axis and F sub two makes an angle of thirty degrees from the x axis in a clockwise direction. A friction force f is equal to seven point five newtons, shown by a vector pointing in negative x direction. In the free-body diagram, F sub one and F sub two are shown by arrows toward the right, making a forty-five degree angle above the horizontal and a thirty-degree angle below the horizontal respectively. The friction force f is shown by an arrow along the negative x axis.
figure.caption: An overhead view of the horizontal forces acting on a child’s snow saucer sled.

exercises.prompt: Two children pull a third child on a snow saucer sled exerting forces $F_1$ and $F_2$ as shown from above in the figure. Find the acceleration of the 49.00-kg sled and child system. Note that the direction of the frictional force is unspecified; it will be in the opposite direction of the sum of $F_1$ and $F_2$.

parts.hint: Project the two pulls onto the east and north axes, add the components axis by axis, then subtract the friction, which opposes their sum.
The direction of the acceleration is the direction of the net force, so take the inverse tangent of the northward component over the eastward one.

figure.alt: Cross-section of jaw with sixteen teeth is shown. Braces are along the outside of the teeth. Three forces are acting on the protruding tooth. A force, T, is shown by an arrow making an angle of fifteen degrees below the positive x axis, and a second force, T, is shown by an arrow making an angle of fifteen degrees below the negative x axis.
figure.caption: Braces are used to apply forces to teeth to realign them. Shown in this figure are the tensions applied by the wire to the protruding tooth. The total force applied to the tooth by the wire, $F_{\text{app}}$, points straight toward the back of the mouth.

exercises.prompt: What force is exerted on the tooth in the figure if the tension in the wire is 25.0 N? Note that the force applied to the tooth is smaller than the tension in the wire, but this is necessitated by practical considerations of how force can be applied in the mouth. Explicitly show how you follow steps in the Problem-Solving Strategy for Newton’s laws of motion.

answer.hint: Take the tooth as the system of interest and choose axes along and across the wire. The two tensions have equal and opposite components along the wire, so only their components across it are left.
answer.solution: 1. Use Newton’s laws since we are looking for forces. 2. Draw a free-body diagram. 3. The tension is given as $T = 25.0\ \text{N}$. Find $F_{\text{app}}$. Using Newton’s laws gives $\Sigma F_y = 0$, so that the applied force is due to the $y$-components of the two tensions: $F_{\text{app}} = 2T\sin\theta = 2(25.0\ \text{N})\sin(15^\circ) = 12.9\ \text{N}$. The $x$-components of the tension cancel: $\sum F_x = 0$. 4. This seems reasonable, since the applied tensions should be greater than the force applied to the tooth.
